name: Annihilation of caste and state socialism

thinkers.name: B. R. Ambedkar
thinkers.note: Economist first, by training: a Columbia PhD and an LSE doctorate on the rupee before he was a jurist or a leader. The economics is not a separate part of the work, and reading the caste writing without it makes the programme look like moral exhortation, which it is not.

claim: Caste is a division of labourers rather than of labour, held in place by endogamy and by religious sanction, and no economic programme that leaves it standing will reach the people at the bottom of it.
summary: Ambedkar's first published work on the subject, a seminar paper written at Columbia in 1916, is about a mechanism. Caste is not simply occupational specialisation. What makes it self-reproducing is endogamy: a rule of marrying within, superimposed on a society that was previously exogamous, which requires a surplus man and a surplus woman in every generation to be disposed of. Sati, enforced widowhood and the marriage of girls are, in his reading, the means by which the boundary is maintained. A caste is a closed class, and closure is the thing to explain.

Annihilation of Caste, written twenty years later as an address he was never allowed to deliver, draws the political conclusion. Caste is graded inequality, which is why it is stable: every group except the lowest has someone beneath it and therefore something to defend. It cannot be dissolved by inter-dining, or by economic reform alone, because its sanction is religious. Ambedkar's demand is against the authority of the shastras themselves, and it is the reason the conference that invited him withdrew the invitation.

The economic programme is set out in States and Minorities in 1947, submitted to the Constituent Assembly on behalf of the Scheduled Castes Federation, and it is more radical than anything in the Congress platform. Key industries owned by the state. Insurance a state monopoly. Agriculture a state industry: land taken over, consolidated, and leased to collective farms worked by village residents without distinction of caste or creed. He called it state socialism, and he wanted it written into the constitution so that no legislature could undo it.

The reason for that programme is caste rather than class. A landless Dalit household given formal equality but no land, in a village where land and credit and labour hiring all run along caste lines, is free in a sense that does not bite. Ambedkar's answer is to remove the asset from the field where caste operates, which is also why he had no patience at all for the village as a unit of self-government.

axis_notes.allocation: State socialism, written as a constitutional obligation rather than a policy. Ambedkar distrusted the market for the same reason he distrusted the village: both were arenas where caste already held the positions.
axis_notes.priority: As far towards redistribute-first as the shelf goes, and explicitly so: political democracy without social democracy beneath it will not last.
axis_notes.hierarchy: The defining position. Hierarchy is a cause with its own machinery, and a purely economic programme is what he spent his career arguing against.
axis_notes.agency: Both, uneasily. Organisation of the oppressed themselves, and a state strong enough to act against the society that produced it. He did not think either alone would do.

layers.title: Endogamy is the mechanism
layers.text: Ambedkar's 1916 argument. Occupational specialisation exists everywhere and does not produce caste. What produces caste is a closed boundary, maintained by marrying within, and the customs that dispose of the surplus spouse in each generation are the enforcement machinery rather than incidental cruelties.

layers.title: The inequality is graded, and that is why it holds
layers.text: Caste is not a line with two sides but an ordered ladder. Every group except the last has one below it, so opposition to the system never assembles: the injury and the interest are distributed along the same scale. Ambedkar returns to this repeatedly as the explanation for why revolt against caste has been so rare and so local.

layers.title: Its sanction is religious, so reform cannot reach it
layers.text: Caste survives because it is believed to be right and not merely because it is convenient. That is why inter-dining and social reform campaigns leave it intact, and why Ambedkar's demand is aimed at the authority of the shastras rather than at particular practices. The Jat-Pat Todak Mandal, having invited him to say caste should go, withdrew the invitation when it read what he proposed to say about the texts.

layers.title: Caste is also a distribution of assets
layers.text: The point that separates Ambedkar from moral critics of caste. Endogamy plus inheritance means land, credit and skill stay inside the boundary across generations. A Dalit household is not merely insulted; it is landless, and it is landless in a village where employment, tenancy and lending are all controlled by the households above it. Formal equality entering that arrangement changes very little.

nodes.label:

layers.title: So the village is the problem, not the solution
layers.text: Ambedkar told the Constituent Assembly that the village was a sink of localism, a den of ignorance and narrow-mindedness, and asked what the village had contributed to the life of the individual living in it. This is aimed directly at Gandhi. Where local self-government is proposed as freedom, Ambedkar reads it as handing administration to precisely the people who already hold the land.

layers.title: The remedy is constitutional and economic together
layers.text: Untouchability abolished by article rather than by campaign. Representation guaranteed. And, in States and Minorities, land taken into state ownership and leased to collective farms worked without distinction of caste, with key industries and insurance owned by the state, all of it entrenched in the constitution so that a legislature could not repeal it. Ambedkar got the first two written in. He did not get the third.

evidence.finding: It has barely moved. The India Human Development Survey found around five per cent of Indian marriages crossing caste boundaries, a figure that has changed little across survey rounds and is low enough that the boundary Ambedkar identified is still doing what he said it does.
evidence.source: India Human Development Survey, NCAER and University of Maryland

evidence.claim: Legal abolition would end the practice of untouchability.
evidence.finding: Article 17 abolished untouchability in 1950 and the practice survives it. In the same survey, around a quarter of households said someone in the household practised untouchability, a figure obtained by asking directly and therefore likely to be an underestimate.
evidence.source: Amit Thorat and Omkar Joshi on IHDS data, Economic and Political Weekly

evidence.claim: Industrial and urban employment dissolves caste.
evidence.finding: Not on its own. Sukhadeo Thorat and Paul Attewell sent matched job applications differing only in the applicant's name to private-sector vacancies and found Dalit and Muslim names called for interview at significantly lower rates than equivalently qualified upper-caste Hindu names. The modern sector reproduced the boundary rather than dissolving it, which is the outcome Ambedkar's theory predicts and Lewis's does not.
evidence.source: Sukhadeo Thorat and Paul Attewell, Economic and Political Weekly

evidence.finding: It has not, in the way the programme required. Land reform in India transferred a small fraction of operated area, ceiling legislation was widely evaded, and the collective farming proposal of States and Minorities was never attempted. Scheduled Caste households remain disproportionately landless and disproportionately dependent on wage labour, which is the condition the programme was designed to end.
evidence.source: Agricultural Census and NSSO land and livestock holding surveys

unsettled: The part of Ambedkar's programme that was adopted is the part that could be written into a constitution, and the part that was not is the economic half. That makes the natural experiment unavailable: nobody can say what state ownership of land leased to caste-mixed collectives would have done, because it was never tried anywhere in India at scale. What the record does show is that the constitutional half alone has produced representation and mobility for some without dissolving the mechanism, which is close to what Ambedkar predicted would happen if the two halves were separated. He said in 1949 that the country was entering a life of contradictions, and named this one.
india: This is the Indian theory that the international shelf usually leaves out, and its absence distorts everything around it. Read next to Lewis or Rostow it identifies exactly what they assume away: that a worker is free to move, that a market hires on productivity, that the village is a neutral container. Read next to Gandhi it is the sharpest disagreement in modern Indian thought, conducted between two people who agreed on independence and on almost nothing about what should follow.
compare_note: Both read Indian development through who holds assets rather than through aggregates, and both expect a state captured by asset-holders to under-deliver.
contrast_note: The central quarrel. Gandhi's village republic is Ambedkar's den of ignorance, and both are describing the same village.
